result: Thbs4 mRNA and protein are induced in dystrophic skeletal muscle from human patients and mouse models, accompanied by markers of ER stress including increased ATF6α-N and BiP levels.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including human patient data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and Western blot data from two mouse models at multiple time points (Figures 1B,C and supplements). The association with ER stress markers is consistently demonstrated across samples.

result: A skeletal muscle-specific Thbs4 transgenic mouse was generated showing differential expression levels across muscle types, with high expression in fast-twitch muscles and no expression in heart.
evaluation: Claims C5-C9 are supported by the transgene schematic and Western blot data in Figure 1D showing tissue-specific expression patterns. The muscle-specific promoter successfully drives differential Thbs4 expression as intended.

result: Thbs4 protein localizes predominantly intracellularly in a vesicular pattern co-localizing with ER markers in healthy transgenic muscle, while in dystrophic muscle it can also be detected in the ECM at sites of fibrosis.
evaluation: Claims C10-C14, C20-C21 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) showing co-localization with calreticulin and differential localization patterns between healthy and diseased muscle. The data consistently demonstrate intracellular vesicular localization in non-diseased conditions.

result: Thbs4 contains glycosylation patterns characteristic of both ER-resident proteins and proteins that transit through the Golgi for secretion.
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by biochemical glycosylation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) using Endo H and PNGase F treatments, which demonstrate both high mannose (ER-type) and complex (Golgi-processed) glycosylation patterns.

result: Extracellular Thbs4 is rapidly internalized by C2C12 myoblasts and myotubes, with myoblast-internalized Thbs4 trafficking to rab7-positive late endosomes.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by in vitro data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing time-dependent uptake of recombinant Thbs4 and co-localization with rab7 in myoblasts. The data provide mechanistic insight into Thbs4 recycling.

result: The myofiber is an important cellular source of Thbs4 expression, secretion, and re-uptake.
evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by the collective evidence from immunofluorescence, biochemical analysis, and in vitro studies (C10-C21), though the authors appropriately note this does not exclude expression by non-muscle cells.

result: Thbs4 overexpression in skeletal muscle induces an ER stress profile similar to dystrophic muscle and causes dramatic expansion of uniform, electron-dense sub-sarcolemmal and intramyofibrillar vesicles containing Thbs4.
evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and transmission electron microscopy with immunogold labeling (Figures 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). The vesicular expansion is quantified and consistently observed.

result: Thbs4 overexpression causes no pathology in wild-type mice but significantly reduces multiple histopathological and functional hallmarks of muscular dystrophy in both Sgcd-/- and mdx mice at 3 and 12 months of age.
evaluation: Claims C26-C34 are supported by comprehensive histological, biochemical, and functional data (Figures 2A-E, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-3) across two disease models and multiple time points. The protective effects are consistently demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis.

result: Thbs4 overexpression significantly reduces membrane rupture after forced treadmill running in dystrophic mice as measured by EBD uptake, with no uptake in wild-type or Thbs4 transgenic mice.
evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by EBD uptake data (Figures 2F,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G) demonstrating reduced sarcolemmal damage in dystrophic mice with Thbs4 overexpression.

result: Thbs4 overexpression induces dramatic sub-sarcolemmal and intramyofibrillar vesicular expansion in dystrophic skeletal muscle of both Sgcd-/- and mdx mice.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by transmission electron microscopy data (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2H) showing consistent vesicular expansion in both dystrophic models.

result: AAV9-mediated Thbs4 overexpression initiated postnatally significantly reduces dystrophic pathology in Sgcd-/- mice, demonstrating therapeutic potential even when treatment is delayed.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by the AAV9 gene therapy experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showing reduced central nucleation and fibrosis when Thbs4 is delivered after birth, providing proof-of-concept for therapeutic intervention.

result: Loss of Thbs4 causes minimal pathology at 3 months in otherwise healthy mice but significantly worsens muscular dystrophy in both Sgcd-/- and mdx backgrounds.
evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by histological, biochemical, and functional data (Figure 3A-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) demonstrating that Thbs4 deletion exacerbates dystrophic pathology in two disease models.

result: Thbs4-/- mice develop age-dependent muscle dysfunction and pathology, showing reduced treadmill performance, elevated serum CK, increased central nucleation, histopathological changes, and greater EBD uptake by 6-12 months of age.
evaluation: Claims C47-C53 are supported by longitudinal functional and histological data (Figure 3F-J) demonstrating progressive muscle pathology with aging in Thbs4-/- mice, establishing Thbs4 as important for maintaining muscle integrity during aging.

result: Thbs4 induction in dystrophic disease and low-level expression during aging represent an adaptive physiologic response that protects skeletal muscle.
evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by the combined evidence that Thbs4 overexpression is protective (C27-C42) while Thbs4 loss worsens disease (C43-C53), establishing Thbs4 as an adaptive protective factor.

result: Thbs4 overexpression protects against lengthening-contraction injury in wild-type and dystrophic muscle, while Thbs4 loss increases susceptibility to such injury.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by functional data from ex vivo lengthening-contraction assays (Figure 4B,C) showing bidirectional effects of Thbs4 on muscle injury resistance across multiple injury cycles.

result: Thbs4 modulates passive muscle elasticity and tendon strength, with increased passive force in Thbs4 Tg and reduced passive force and weaker tendons in Thbs4-/- mice, though twitch force is unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by biomechanical measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing Thbs4-dependent effects on passive mechanical properties without affecting active force generation.

result: Thbs4 overexpression reduces membrane damage and enhances repair in isolated myofibers after laser injury, while Thbs4 loss increases damage, with effects demonstrated in both wild-type and dystrophic backgrounds.
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by FM1-43 dye uptake assays in isolated FDB myofibers (Figure 4D-F), demonstrating cell-autonomous effects of Thbs4 on membrane stability independent of ECM attachments.

result: Thbs4 provides sarcolemmal stability through intracellular mechanisms, as demonstrated by protection in isolated myofibers lacking ECM attachments.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by the laser injury experiments in isolated myofibers (C63-C67), which demonstrate that Thbs4 functions from within the myofiber to stabilize the membrane, independent of extracellular matrix connections.

result: Thbs4 accelerates both ER-to-Golgi and Golgi-to-membrane vesicular trafficking in an ATF6α-dependent manner, as demonstrated by FRAP and iFRAP assays.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by live-cell FRAP/iFRAP experiments (Figure 5A-D) showing accelerated trafficking with Thbs4 overexpression, inhibition by dominant-negative ATF6α, and mimicry by constitutively active ATF6α.

result: The Type III repeat (T3R) domain of Thbs4, which interacts with ATF6α, is necessary and sufficient for accelerating vesicular trafficking, while the LamG domain and related protein Nell2 are not.
evaluation: Claims C76-C81 are supported by domain-specific FRAP/iFRAP experiments (Figure 5E-J) demonstrating that the T3R domain alone can accelerate trafficking while other domains cannot, establishing structure-function relationships.

result: Thbs4 overexpression increases levels of trafficking regulatory proteins including Sar1, Rab24, Rab6, Rab3, and Rab8 in skeletal muscle.
evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) showing increased expression of multiple Rab proteins and Sar1 that regulate ER-to-Golgi and post-Golgi trafficking.

result: Thbs4 accelerates intracellular vesicular trafficking through an ATF6α-dependent mechanism, potentially enhancing membrane stability by increasing vesicular flux to the sarcolemma.
evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by the collective trafficking data (C71-C82) demonstrating ATF6α-dependent acceleration of vesicular trafficking by Thbs4, providing a mechanistic link to membrane stabilization.

result: Thbs4 overexpression increases sarcolemmal localization of dystrophin-glycoprotein complex components and integrins in both wild-type and dystrophic muscle, partially rescuing sarcoglycan localization in Sgcd-/- mice.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6A) showing increased membrane localization of multiple DGC and integrin components with Thbs4 overexpression, including partial rescue of sarcoglycans in Sgcd-/- background.

result: Thbs4 overexpression increases membrane levels of utrophin, dystroglycans, and multiple integrins in wild-type, Sgcd-/-, and mdx muscle as measured by Western blotting of membrane-enriched fractions.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by Western blot analysis of sarcolemmal protein preparations (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) showing increased membrane residency of attachment complex proteins across multiple genotypes.

result: Thbs4 increases membrane localization of integrins without increasing total cellular protein levels, indicating enhanced trafficking rather than increased synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by Western blot comparison of membrane versus total protein extracts (Figure 6B) showing increased membrane levels without corresponding increases in total protein, supporting a trafficking mechanism.

result: Loss of Thbs4 reduces membrane residency of dystroglycans and integrins in skeletal muscle.
evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by Western blot data from Thbs4-/- muscle (Figure 6C) showing reduced membrane levels of multiple attachment proteins, providing loss-of-function evidence complementing the gain-of-function studies.

result: Thbs4 regulates membrane stability by augmenting trafficking of membrane attachment protein complexes to the sarcolemma.
evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by the collective evidence from membrane protein localization studies (C84-C94) and trafficking assays (C71-C83), establishing a comprehensive mechanism for Thbs4 function.

result: Thbs4 directly binds β1D-integrin but not α7-integrin intracellularly, and co-localizes with α5-integrin in β1D-integrin-positive vesicles.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E) demonstrating selective Thbs4-integrin interactions and co-localization in intracellular vesicles.

result: Skeletal muscle-specific ATF6α overexpression induces ER stress markers and causes dramatic ER and vesicular expansion without pathology, with vesicles appearing less dense than those in Thbs4 transgenic mice.
evaluation: Claims C99-C104 are supported by Western blot and electron microscopy data (Figure 7A-D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing that ATF6α overexpression recapitulates some but not all features of Thbs4 overexpression.

result: ATF6α overexpression provides no protection against muscular dystrophy and does not increase sarcolemmal localization of membrane attachment proteins.
evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by comprehensive histological, functional, and biochemical data (Figure 7E-K, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) demonstrating that ATF6α alone is insufficient for protection despite inducing vesicular expansion.

result: ATF6α is only one component of the mechanism by which Thbs4 regulates membrane stability, as ATF6α overexpression alone does not recapitulate Thbs4's protective effects.
evaluation: Claim C107 is supported by the observation that ATF6α overexpression induces vesicular expansion but fails to protect against dystrophy or increase membrane attachment proteins (C105-C106), indicating additional Thbs4 functions beyond ATF6α activation.

result: Secretion-competent full-length Thbs4, but not ER-retained Thbs4 mutant, promotes β1 integrin membrane occupancy, indicating Thbs4 must transit through the secretory pathway to chaperone integrins.
evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by in vivo adenoviral experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 3) comparing secretion-competent versus ER-retained Thbs4, demonstrating the requirement for secretory pathway transit.

result: Drosophila possess a single Tsp gene that causes embryonic lethality when deficient due to muscle-tendon attachment ruptures, and Tsp interacts with αPS2/βPS integrin.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by citations to prior work (Subramanian et al., 2007; Chanana et al., 2007), establishing the evolutionary conservation of thrombospondin function in muscle attachment.

result: Both mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp rescue lifespan, muscle function, and muscle-tendon attachment defects in the Sgcd840 Drosophila muscular dystrophy model.
evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by survival curves, negative geotaxis assays, and histological data (Figure 8A-C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C) demonstrating functional conservation of thrombospondin protection across species.

result: Mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp overexpression in Drosophila muscle is restricted to intracellular vesicles and increases membrane βPS integrin localization.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are supported by immunofluorescence, immunogold EM, and Western blot data (Figure 8D-F, H, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D-F) showing intracellular localization and increased integrin membrane levels in Drosophila.

result: Mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp overexpression rescues sarcomeric tears in Sgcd840 Drosophila without inducing ER stress or vesicular expansion.
evaluation: Claims C117-C118 are supported by electron microscopy and Western blot data (Figure 8F-G, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G-I) showing structural rescue without ER stress induction, indicating phylogenetic differences in mechanism.

result: Thrombospondin proteins represent an evolutionarily ancient program for membrane stabilization through regulation of intracellular attachment complexes, while ER expansion through ATF6α evolved after Drosophila.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by the conservation of Thbs/Tsp function in membrane stabilization and integrin trafficking across mice and Drosophila (C112-C118), combined with the absence of ER expansion in Drosophila, indicating phylogenetic evolution of the ATF6α component.
